To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

radiation dose can be reduced for CT-guided interventions by using a combination of technical strategies that include the use of alternative guidance methods, restriction of scan field of view, use of low tube current, and the use of CT fluoroscopy.

radiation dose can be reduced for CT-guided procedures in the abdomen by limiting the scan length to the interventional region, using low tube currents, choosing dose efficient modes, and minimizing the use of CT fluoroscopy.

CT fluoroscopy can be safely and effectively performed with a tube current of 10-20 mA and that CT fluoroscope guidance can be safely performed with a tube voltage of 80 kVp and a tube current of up to 20 mA.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new techniques for radiation dose reduction in CT-guided interstitial brachytherapy of prostate cancer.
the development of new methods to improve the quality of CT images and to reduce the radiation dose for diagnostic imaging and CT guided interventions.
the development of new methods for the analysis, design and optimization of CT-guided inter- ventional procedures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
radiation dose reduction is feasible and should be a priority for CT-guided procedures in the abdomen or pelvis.
dose reduction is best accomplished by using the lowest radiation dose necessary to accomplish the clinical task at hand.

dose optimization for these procedures can be achieved through the use of low tube current and low dose efficient scanning modes for diagnostic CT, intermittent mode, narrow collimated CT fluoroscopic guidance, and limiting the cranio-caudoal length of the interventional scan to the interventional area.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that radiation dose reduction is possible in the majority of patients undergoing CT-guided interstitial radiofrequency ablations of liver tumors and renal cell carcinoma.
the radiation dose to patients can often be significantly reduced by using CT fluoroscopy with intermittent scanning and low tube current, and by limiting the length of the interventional CT scan.
the use of CT for guidance of interventional procedures in patients with cancer is safe when radiation dose is optimized.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dose from CT-guided interstitial procedures can be reduced by 50% or more without compromising image quality or the ability to perform the procedure.
CT-guided interstitial tumor ablation procedures can be performed with radiation dose levels that are similar to those for diagnostic CT scans, and in many cases lower.
radiation dose optimization for these procedures should not be left up to the interventional radiologists.
